When deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock, investors often rely on analyst recommendations. Media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts often influence a stock's price, but are they really important?

Before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage, let's see what these Wall Street heavyweights think about Cloudflare (NET).

Cloudflare currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.56, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 32 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.56 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.

Of the 32 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 23 are Strong Buy and two are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 71.9% and 6.3% of all recommendations.

Brokerage Recommendation Trends for NET
Broker Rating Breakdown Chart for NET

Check price target & stock forecast for Cloudflare here>>>

The ABR suggests buying Cloudflare, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.

Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation.

This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, which classifies stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), is a reliable indicator of a stock's near-term price performance. So, validating the Zacks Rank with ABR could go a long way in making a profitable investment decision.

Zacks Rank Should Not Be Confused With ABR

In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures.

The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.

title: Jim Cramer Calls Cloudflare “the Most Expensive Stock in the Market.” He Still Prefers It

Jim Cramer Calls Cloudflare “the Most Expensive Stock in the Market.” He Still Prefers It

Explore stocks on Coinbase

Jim Cramer Calls Cloudflare "the Most Expensive Stock in the Market." He Still Prefers It ©@da-kuk from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Jim Cramer told a Mad Money caller he likes Cloudflare more than Akamai, even though he called Cloudflare "the most expensive stock in the market."

Cloudflare trades at 169x forward earnings against 12x for Akamai, after growing 39% in the third quarter while Akamai grew 6%.

Cloudflare booked its first Act 4 revenue in the third quarter, including payments for helping OpenAI crawl more efficiently, but hasn't disclosed the amount.

On Monday's Mad Money, Jim Cramer took a call from a viewer who'd bought Akamai Technologies (AKAM:NASDAQ) at $103 and watched it slide to $78.

Cramer blamed the slide on a convertible bond sale ("they did this big convertible bond and everyone's running from it"). That same day, Akamai announced $2.2 billion of convertible notes, and the stock closed at $80.29.

Then he pivoted to Akamai's pricier rival, Cloudflare (NET:NYSE), and its CEO, Matthew Prince, whom he called "the real deal."

"I think that Cloudflare, even though it's the most expensive stock in the market, I like more than I like Akamai," he said.

Cramer's Right About Cloudflare's Price

Cloudflare trades at 169x its expected earnings over the next 12 months. Akamai trades at 12x, even after landing an $11.6 billion compute deal with Anthropic in September.

Most of that gap is growth. Cloudflare's third-quarter revenue rose 39% to $782.5 million, its fastest growth in nearly four years, while Akamai's rose 6% to $1.12 billion. And Cloudflare has been priced like this for years: 169x is close to its 173x average at quarter-ends since mid-2023.

Analysts Already Expect a Lot

Analysts expect Cloudflare's revenue to rise from $2.17 billion in 2025 to $5.09 billion in 2028, about 31% a year in both 2027 and 2028.

NET Revenue Estimates: 2023-2028 (TIKR)

That's full-year revenue, while management's goal is $5 billion in annualized revenue by the fourth quarter of 2028. A full year at $5.09 billion implies a fourth-quarter pace above that goal, so to justify 169x, Cloudflare has to beat estimates that already run ahead of its own target.

AI agents are the reason it might. Cloudflare said on its second-quarter call that non-human traffic passed human traffic on its network in May, and that if trends hold it could reach 1,000 times human traffic within five years.

Traffic only helps if someone pays for it. Cloudflare calls its effort to develop new internet business models Act 4, and Prince said the company recorded its first Act 4 revenue in the third quarter, including a service that helps OpenAI crawl more efficiently. It hasn't disclosed the amount. Carrying more traffic also costs money: GAAP gross margin fell to 71.2% in the third quarter from 74.0% a year earlier.

Cloudflare reported third quarter 2026 revenue of US$782.51 million and a net loss of US$34.07 million, raised fourth quarter and full year sales guidance, and highlighted broad demand across developer infrastructure and AI related security.

The appointment of Christian Smith as President of Revenue adds a seasoned go to market leader with experience scaling recurring revenue businesses and managing complex enterprise sales motions at scale.

The focus now turns to how Cloudflare's stronger top line guidance and accelerated profitability timeline may influence the longer term investment narrative.

Compare Cloudflare's earnings momentum with other infrastructure and security plays by exploring a curated set of 53 AI infrastructure stocks that may be preparing for their next big move.

Cloudflare Investment Narrative Recap

To own Cloudflare, you need to believe in its role as critical internet plumbing for security, developer workloads, and AI heavy traffic. According to DaneDruss, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the thesis leans on Cloudflare as a migration and trust layer rather than a pure compute play. The latest quarter shows revenue at US$782.51 million and a continued net loss of US$34.07 million, so the near-term catalyst is execution on the path to GAAP profitability while keeping growth intact.

The biggest operational risk right now is that costs tied to growth and AI security use cases keep pressure on margins. Management has talked about a faster GAAP profit timeline, so any stumble on expenses or gross margin could matter more than headline sales beats. On the positive side, raised full year revenue guidance toward about US$3.0 billion provides some evidence that customer demand across security and developer tools is broad rather than concentrated in a few AI buyers.

The appointment of Christian Smith as President of Revenue is the announcement that ties most directly to these catalysts. His remit covers Cloudflare's global go-to-market engine, including sales, renewals, revenue operations, and partnerships. Smith previously helped scale annual recurring revenue above US$4.0 billion at Splunk while managing a shift to cloud and subscription, which is relevant to where Cloudflare is aiming to go on usage-based services.

For shareholders, the key question is whether this hire improves execution against the US$5.0 billion ARR ambition and supports cleaner unit economics. Better sales discipline and a tighter Unified Engagement style model could help convert large security and developer interest into longer contracts and deeper product adoption. The risk is that a bigger commercial footprint adds cost and complexity just as investors are watching profitability, so progress on operating leverage will be important to track alongside any future AI and post-quantum security traction that DaneDruss expects could influence customer trust.

Key Takeaways

Datadog stock fell 17% in a week after a roughly flat fourth-quarter revenue guide outweighed 35% third-quarter growth.

The guide counts its largest customer, an AI company that cut its usage, only at its contract minimum.

Cloudflare's fourth-quarter guide keeps climbing, a sign the slowdown may be confined to one Datadog account.

At about 60x forward earnings, far below its usual multiple, Datadog looks like a buy ahead of February's 2027 outlook.

Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) stock fell 17% in the week through Nov. 9, and most of it traces back to one customer.

Citi analyst Fatima Boolani says the selloff is "likely missing forest-for-the-trees." Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) backs her up: its own outlook, out a day after Datadog's, keeps climbing.

Great quarter, flat outlook

Datadog reported before the open on Nov. 4. Revenue rose 35% to $1.20 billion, $52 million above the top of its own range, and adjusted EPS of $0.81 beat the $0.64 consensus. But fourth-quarter revenue is guided to 1.19-1.20 billion, roughly flat with the quarter it just reported, or 25% to 26% growth from a year earlier. Shares fell 14% that day and slid further on Thursday, Nov. 5, as the Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.5%.

Outside one customer, growth is speeding up

CFO David Obstler said on the third-quarter call that the largest customer cut its usage, though it still spent above its minimum commitment, and the guide counts it only at that minimum. Strip it out, and fourth-quarter growth comes to the low to mid 30s, even as some big customers, AI accounts included, renewed early for bigger commitments at better volume pricing. Growth outside AI customers sped up for a fifth straight quarter, to the high 20s, and Datadog now has more than 850 AI customers.

Cloudflare's third-quarter revenue rose 39% to $782.5 million, and it guided the fourth quarter to 845-846 million, another step up. Its shares jumped 9.9% on Nov. 6. A broad pullback in cloud spending would likely have shown up there too.
